newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian PM stands firm despite more protests.
newsitem.headline: Albanian PM stands firm despite more protests.

text.p: Albania's right-wing government showed no sign of yielding on Friday despite violent protests in the capital over the collapse of popular investment schemes which left thousands of people penniless.
Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi told Reuters he was ready to resign over the crisis if his ruling Democratic Party asked him to, but quickly added he had the party's full support.
Albania has been racked by protests and riots for five weeks, with demonstrators demanding the government reimburse them for millions of dollars of lost savings and then resign.
Violence erupted in Tirana, capital of the Balkan country of 3.4 million people, for the first time on Thursday when scores of protesters hurled stones at police.
Police threw the stones back at the protesters, who had been trying to march to central Skanderbeg Square after a peaceful opposition party rally.
An angry crowd of several hundred people dispersed after police fired shots in the air and waded in with truncheons flailing.
Some 7,000 people marched for a 17th day in the southern port town of Vlore, where three people died last week and 150 were injured during clashes with riot police.
A desperate woman with three children started crying at the Vlore University stairs as marchers streamed past, saying she had lost everything in the schemes and had no way to live.
People pushed past several dozen policemen guarding the university and filled a plastic bag with small banknotes to help her.
Fifty-five university students began a hunger strike on Thursday to demand the government resign for its handling of the pyramid scandal and for sending riot police against Vlore protesters.

Tens of thousands of Albanians lost large sums of money when five fraudulent pyramid schemes collapsed last month. The schemes used new money, pumped in at a frenzied pace in recent months, to cover high-interest payments due on older debts.
The collapse, with some $1 to $2 billion invested in the schemes, dealt a heavy blow to the new free market economy which has emerged since the fall of a Stalinist regime 1990.
It has also posed the most serious crisis for Meksi and President Sali Berisha since they came to power in 1992 on pledges of rapid economic growth and free market reforms.
Almost every family in the country has been hurt in the pyramids. Angry investors blame Berisha and Meksi for failing to regulate the schemes and failing to warn of their dangers.
Berisha kept up a cross-country campaign on Friday to try to win back support. He has spent the week publicly admitting he made mistakes and pledging to push economic growth.
After addresses to selected supporters in Tirana and other towns, he travelled to Peshkopi on Friday in the rugged inland mountains of the north to shore up support there.
Berisha has sought to dominate evening television news with supporters in sports halls or theatres chanting "Sali Berisha".

Cracks have opened in his Democratic Party with 14 deputies in parliament calling on Thursday for Meksi to resign. Meksi dismissed the call and said critics could leave the party if they opposed its policies.
"They have a right to their opinion and they have the right not to stay with us at this difficult moment," he told Reuters.
He said the violent protests in Tirana on Thursday were the work of left-wing extremists linked to Albania's Stalinist past.
"They want to provoke us. They are speaking for democracy but they are not democrats," Meksi said. "They have the books of Lenin, Marx and Enver Hoxha -- they are for the proletarian revolution."
Hoxha ruled Albania with a iron fist for 45 years, keeping the country impoverished and isolated. He died in 1985.
Hundreds of ruined investors swarmed around Albania's largest investment holding company for a second day on Friday in the hope of getting their money back.
The Vefa company, with 80,000 investors and 240 businesses, froze all acounts after the fraudulent pyramids collapsed. It said this week it would return the capital of small investors.

"We are asking only for what we earned with our backs and blood as illegal workers in foreign countries. We just want our money," said Shefget Gjoka, 30. He put $10,000 at Vefa, saved during four years working construction in Greece.
